title: Give figures, mermaid and table headers what PDF/UA needs
description: PAC reports 13 text-alternative failures on a 0.12.0 deck. All 13 are <figure> wrappers that Chromium tags /Figure with no /Alt; five of those wrap mermaid diagrams that have no accessible name at all. Separately, all 20 <th> reach the PDF with /Scope: None. These three are fixable in the templates; the rest of what PAC found is not.
design: THE THREE THAT ARE FIXABLE IN HTML Split out of stn-ips, which measured them. That ticket is the check; this one is the repair. Between them they should take PAC's 1.1 row from 13 failures to 0, which is the only row a template change can clear outright. 1. THE
acceptance_criteria: A generated PDF has no /Figure lacking /Alt or /ActualText. Mermaid diagrams carry their caption as an accessible name. Every /TH carries a /Scope. All three asserted against a built PDF's structure tree, not against the DOM.
notes:
Shipped in 0.15.0 (PR #54, d158f6f, tagged v0.15.0).

TWO OF THE THREE WERE REAL. THE THIRD DID NOT REPRODUCE.

1. <figure> tagged /Figure with no /Alt -- CONFIRMED, exactly as recorded.
   21 /Figure, 8 named, 13 not, and the 13 are the <figure> elements.

2. Mermaid diagrams unnamed -- CONFIRMED, and fixed on both sides.

3. <th> with /Scope: None -- DID NOT REPRODUCE. Measured on the same
   kanban-and-sdd.pdf the ticket cites: all 20 /TH carry /Scope /Column.
   Chromium infers it from <thead>, and infers /Row for a row-header table
   (measured separately). No Lua filter was added. A test now pins it, because
   the inference depends on table shape and a table with no <thead> would lose
   it silently.

THE CANDIDATE THAT LOOKS RIGHT AND IS A DELETION

The ticket listed role="none" on the <figure> as a candidate. Measured, it
clears the failure by removing the unnamed /Figure -- and a mermaid figure's
<svg> is not tagged either, so the diagram leaves the structure tree entirely
rather than being named. Zero failures, one fewer diagram. Only building the
PDF and reading its tag tree distinguishes it from the real fix.

Chosen instead: aria-labelledby on the <figure> pointing at its own caption, so
the name derives from text already on the page. aria-label works identically in
the tag tree but duplicates the string.

FOUND WHILE WIRING IT

- pandoc.Caption takes BLOCKS first and was being handed inlines. pandoc
  coerced the list, so every Str and Space became a block: one <figcaption>
  holding four of them.
- The default caption was used but never written back to the block, so
  data-caption -- what the page script names the diagram with -- existed only
  when an author had written a caption.
- caption="" produced a figure with an empty <figcaption> and NO accessible
  name: in Lua the empty string is truthy, so `'' or 'Diagram'` is ''. That is
  this ticket's own failure, reachable through the most natural way to ask for
  no caption. Both found by local CodeRabbit after the main fix was written.

VERIFICATION

Against the built PDF's structure tree, never the DOM -- a DOM assertion is what
would have passed while the PDF stayed broken. Four breaches, each failing only
its own tests: unregister the filter (2), drop role=img (1), revert the caption
block structure (1), revert the caption normalization (3).

The caption-structure test is the one deliberate DOM assertion, and says why:
the PDF text layer does not distinguish one block from four, measured, for the
same reason 0.13.0's header ran words together.

448 tests, up from 439. pa11y clean in both themes.
close_reason: Closed

Reported WCAG tab: 1.1 Text Alternatives 8 pass 0 warn 13 FAIL 1.3 Adaptable 46881 pass 3 warn 1177 FAIL 1.4 Distinguishable 18107 pass 0 warn 72 FAIL 2.4 Navigable 1 pass 0 warn 2 FAIL 3.1 Readable 21360 pass 0 warn 0 pass 4.1 Compatible 2362 pass 13 warn 31 FAIL Walking the PDF's own structure tree reproduces the two largest rows exactly. 1.1, ACCOUNTED FOR PRECISELY. The markup carries 13
acceptance_criteria: A check in the repository opens a PDF and reports conformance, runnable as a make target beside check-access. The target profile is a recorded decision -- conformance or no-regression-against-baseline -- not left implicit. The known-unfixable-from-HTML items (/LBody, /NonStruct density) are written down as accepted or as a pipeline decision, so a later reader does not re-derive them.
notes:
BATCHING (asked during triage)

Yes -- one container run, many PDFs. veraPDF's documentation calls batch
processing a primary use case ("the best way of processing batches of PDF
files") and documents validating every file in a folder, plus validating
against several profiles in one go.

This matters more than it sounds. veraPDF is a JVM tool, so process startup
dominates for small inputs; paying it once for a whole package is the
difference between a check people run and one they skip.

NOT VERIFIED, and worth confirming with `verapdf --help` the first time the
image is built rather than trusting a summary: the exact operand syntax
(multiple paths vs a directory), the recursion flag, the flavour flag for
PDF/UA-1, the output-format flag, and the exit code on non-conformance. The
exit code is the one that actually gates the make target, so check it directly.

Note the contrast with the existing check-access, which is the "loop inside the
container" shape already: `for f in *.html` with a pa11y invocation per file
per theme, and pa11y launches a fresh Chromium every time. That is 2N browser
starts for N pages. veraPDF should not need the same treatment -- prefer
handing it the whole set in one invocation, and only fall back to a shell loop
if the CLI turns out to want it.

description: Move header spaces inside their adjacent inline boxes so they reach the PDF text layer, and add PDF-side accessibility assertions

Each guard is proven against its own breach before it is kept: reintroduce the jam (restore the template's inter-element space), watch the new assertion fail, restore. title: A document's subtitle printed larger than its title
description:
The @media print block scales .doc-title to 18pt and .doc-meta to 10pt but never mentioned .doc-subtitle, which kept its screen value of 1.8rem. rem is measured against the root font size, not against the title beside it, so the subtitle printed at 21.6pt against the title's 18pt -- the student's name 20% larger than the assignment it belonged to.

Measured off a real hs2.pdf from cs234: title 24.0, subtitle 28.8.

Only the PDF was wrong, which is why it lasted. On screen the two were 2.2rem and 1.8rem, so the title was larger -- but only by 18%, and both were font-weight 700, which is not a hierarchy. The subtitle line is usually the longer of the two, so it took more space than the title and drew the eye.

The decks had this right from the first commit that introduced both: .deck-title 2.9rem/700 over .deck-subtitle 1.5rem with no weight of its own, a ratio of 0.52. The document rule has never changed since it was written.

Reported by the maintainer against hs2-Web-Intro.
acceptance_criteria: In the PDF the title draws at a larger font size than the subtitle, asserted against a real rendered PDF. On screen the subtitle is clearly subordinate rather than merely smaller, and does not match the title for weight. The subtitle stays larger than the byline.
close_reason:
Root cause was the print block naming some selectors and not their neighbours, so a pt size sat beside a rem one. Fixed in three places: .doc-subtitle gets a print size (13pt), h4/h5/h6 get print sizes (11/10.5/10pt) where the scale used to invert at h4, and h1-h6 get explicit screen sizes instead of inheriting Bootstrap's viewport-relative scale, which had h1 at 39.4px above the title's 35.2px. The subtitle also drops to 1.4rem/400 from 1.8rem/700 so it reads as subordinate rather than as a second title.

Verified on the reporter's own file: hs2.pdf title 24.0 / subtitle 17.3, was 24.0 / 28.8. Ten tests in tests/test_title_block.py, two of them measuring a real PDF; mutation-verified by removing each rule in turn. 186 tests pass, integration included.

title: A package_sources-only doc package generates orphaned files and a pkg target that cannot run
description:
generate_package keys the shared page files off has_pages, which includes
package_sources, while get_generated_files and the doc-template injection both
key off docs/slides only. A doc package configured with package_sources and no
docs or slides falls in the gap twice.

1. Invisible generated files.
   generate.py:264 injects hidden-filter.lua, mermaid-figure-filter.lua,
   embed-images.lua, html-to-pdf.js and Dockerfile.browser whenever has_pages is
   true (generate.py:181 = docs or slides or package_sources).
   get_generated_files (generate.py:393) adds them only when
   `package.get("docs") or package.get("slides")`.

   Consequence: those five files are generated but invisible to `clean` and to
   the managed .gitignore section. They show up as untracked files in a course
   repo forever, and nothing removes them.

2. A pkg target that cannot run.
   html-template.html is injected only under `if context.get("has_docs")`
   (generate.py:275). But Makefile-pkg.j2:69 builds PKG_HTML with
   `$(DC) run --rm doc ...`, and pipeline.py:61 makes the doc service pass
   `--template=html-template.html`.

   Consequence: a package_sources-only doc package generates a `pkg` target
   whose pandoc invocation names a template that was never written. The target
   exists and fails.

Both edges are the same mistake: a predicate that says "this package renders
markdown" in one place and "this package has docs or slides" in the other. The
fix in both places is the same -- key the shared files off has_pages and the doc
template off has_pages / has_package_sources rather than has_docs.

Worth noting that has_package_sources (generate.py:168) is already
`bool(package_sources) and package_type == "doc"`, so the predicate needed for
the second half exists and is simply not the one used.

Found by an external review of the repository; both halves verified against the
code before filing. Not yet reproduced end to end -- the first task should be a
failing test that configures a package_sources-only doc package and asserts on
get_generated_files and on the rendered Makefile.
acceptance_criteria:
A doc package configured with package_sources and neither docs nor slides:

- get_generated_files lists the five shared page files, so `clean` removes them
  and the managed .gitignore section covers them.
- html-template.html is generated, so the `pkg` target's pandoc invocation names
  a template that exists.
- Both are covered by tests that fail if either predicate is changed back.

No behaviour change for packages that do declare docs or slides.
close_reason: get_generated_files now reads the derived context it already builds rather than re-spelling the predicates off raw config keys, and the doc template is injected for has_docs or has_package_sources. A package_sources-only doc package gets html-template.html and has all five shared page files covered by clean and the managed .gitignore. Six new tests in test_package_sources.py; verified RED against the old predicates before the fix (7 failures, exactly the two reported halves) and GREEN after, with the other 114 unit tests unchanged.

title: Regression test: a failed asset fails the PDF build instead of degrading it
description:
The generated pages are not self-contained. embed-images.lua inlines images, but Bootstrap, highlight.js, Mermaid and the webfonts are all fetched from CDNs when the page loads. A dropped request does not stop rendering -- it produces a finished-looking PDF with no diagrams, no syntax highlighting and fallback fonts.

html-to-pdf.js collects requestfailed, HTTP >= 400 and pageerror events and refuses to write the file, matching the --fail-if-warnings stance the pandoc services take. It checks twice on purpose: once right after load and once before printing. Mermaid is itself a CDN import, so a dead CDN means __mermaidReady never gets set, and checking only at the end would report a 120s timeout instead of the actual cause.

Both the refusal and the early check should be tested; the early check is easy to lose in a refactor and its absence only shows up as a slow, confusing failure.
acceptance_criteria: A test points the converter at an HTML file with an unresolvable asset reference and asserts a non-zero exit, no PDF on disk, and the failed URL named in stderr. A second assertion covers the fail-fast path: the failure is reported without waiting out the ready-flag timeout.
close_reason: PDF integration tests added. Geometry verified sensitive to the @page rules; fail-fast verified by removing the early check (122s vs 3s). title: Regression test: the PDF waits for client-side rendering before printing
description:
Mermaid renders in the browser, and _page-scripts.html.j2 only assembles the Bootstrap tab panes after dispatching mermaid-ready. html-to-pdf.js waits on window.__mermaidReady to avoid printing the page mid-build.

Two failure modes, neither visible in the HTML:

1. If the wait is removed, a PDF captures raw mermaid source sitting in a code block and tab content that never got moved into its pane. The HTML is still perfect; only the PDF is wrong.
2. If _page-scripts.html.j2 stops setting the flag, every PDF build hangs for the full 120s timeout instead of failing usefully.

The second is the reason the flag deserves a test rather than a comment: it is a contract between two templates that no build step checks.

title: Regression test: PDF page geometry comes from the print stylesheet
description:
html-to-pdf.js prints with preferCSSPageSize, so the @page rules in _page-style.css.j2 and _slide-style.css.j2 are the page geometry -- not a hint, and not something the browser overrides. Documents must come out letter portrait with 1in margins; decks must come out letter landscape with exactly one slide per page.

Nothing enforces this. Drop preferCSSPageSize, or edit an @page block, and the PDFs silently repaginate: a deck can fold two slides onto a page or spill one across two, and neither the build nor the HTML output changes at all.

This is an integration test -- it needs the container, unlike the argv assertions -- so it belongs behind the same marker used for the pandoc build tests.

title: Template test: the pdf target wires OUTPUT_SUFFIX and its dependencies correctly
description:
Docker-free counterpart to the pandoc argv tests: assert on the rendered Makefile text rather than on a build.

Three contracts, all currently defended by nothing:

1. $(OUTPUT_SUFFIX) appears on BOTH sides of each pdf conversion. If it is dropped from one side, 'make pdf with=hidden' prints the plain HTML into the -hidden PDF, or the -hidden HTML into the plain one. The output looks fine; it is just the wrong document, which is the worst possible failure for an answer-key build.
2. pdf depends on doc, so a PDF is never printed from stale HTML left over from a previous run.
3. clean-pkg removes the .pdf and -*.pdf globs alongside the .html ones.

Also worth asserting that the pdf target exists for any package with docs or slides and is absent otherwise, since it is gated on has_pages with no config key.
acceptance_criteria: A test renders Makefile.j2 for a package with both docs and slides and asserts the pdf recipe pairs matching suffixes, depends on doc, and that clean-pkg covers the pdf globs. Fails if OUTPUT_SUFFIX is removed from either side.

Container startup is roughly 0.1s and is not worth removing. Process startup is
not the cost either. The cost is the per-file work -- pandoc parsing, Chromium
loading a multi-megabyte self-contained page, mermaid drawing, fonts -- and
batching cannot remove any of it. Do not build the batching machinery; it buys
about a second per package and adds a moving part to two make targets.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT DID FIND

ex-kanban-management.md contains zero mermaid blocks. Its HTML is 5.19 MB, of
which 3.57 MB is the mermaid bundle it never calls. Same for
ex-kanban-vs-scrum.md. Every document stencil generates carries mermaid whether
or not it draws a diagram.

  with mermaid bundle     1776ms / 1738ms
  without                 1756ms / 1762ms

Identical. V8 does not pay for a script it never runs, so the bundle is free at
build time.

or copied to a flash drive". A 5 MB attachment that should be 1.6 MB is three

cheap. renderMermaid() reads `globalThis.mermaid` into a const but returns on
an empty node list before dereferencing it, so a page with no .mermaid elements
never touches the global. That is why the measurement above completed in 1.7s
rather than timing out on the __mermaidReady handshake.

So the work is: decide per document whether any mermaid block is present, and
inline the bundle only then. The decision has to reach the template -- most
naturally as a flag the lua filter or the generator sets -- and the
__mermaidReady flag must still be set on a page without the bundle, or
html-to-pdf.js waits its full two-minute timeout for a handshake that never
comes.

description: embed-images.lua handles one source per image. A -dark sibling convention would let a figure follow the theme, with the dark rule inside the sealed @media screen block so PDFs keep the light variant for free.
design: WHY THIS CAME UP classroom/kanban/kanban-and-sdd.md in the consuming course repository is now half-themed. It carries five mermaid blocks and eight static matplotlib SVGs. Since 0.12.0 the mermaid diagrams redraw to follow the theme; the SVGs do not. In dark mode the diagrams recolour while the figures stay white-plate. blockquote, link), rendered through html-to-pdf.js.

    heading structure and reading order survive.
  /Lang = en, from <html lang>. WCAG 3.1.1 holds in the PDF.
  /ViewerPreferences /DisplayDocTitle true, which PDF/UA requires.

  "DueSep 12" and "Grim·Ada Lovelace". The HTML has real space characters
  there -- 0.12.0 fixed exactly that for copy-paste and BeautifulSoup -- but
  Chromium renders some inter-element spaces as glyph positioning rather than
  a space glyph, so the PDF text layer jams them back together.

  reader, gets run-on words in the header. The rendered page looks correct.

  repository looks at a PDF. So "the PDFs pass WCAG" is currently unverified
  rather than verified-good, and the tagging above is Chromium's default
  rather than anything this project asserts.

  1. Add a PDF check to the pipeline -- veraPDF for PDF/UA, or a targeted
     assertion on extracted text of the kind tests/test_pdf.py already makes.
     The cheap first move is asserting the header extracts as words, since
     that is the one concrete defect measured here.
  2. Fix the spacing. Likely needs the gaps to be characters Chromium must
     emit -- a non-breaking space in the label, as the fact separators already
     use -- rather than margin or an inter-element space.

Worth doing before anyone relies on the PDFs for accessibility compliance
rather than for printing.

title: bd reopen writes no status transition to the interaction journal
description: bd close journals a status field_change; bd reopen changes the status but records nothing. The interaction log for any reopened issue therefore shows a transition out of a state it was never recorded as leaving.
design: Reproduced on bd 1.2.2: create an issue, bd close it, bd reopen it. The journal holds only 'open -> closed'; the issue's status is then 'open' with no second record. Seen first on stn-49v, whose log reads open -> in_progress -> closed, then open -> in_progress with nothing bridging closed -> open. This is a beads bug, not export corruption -- .beads/interactions.jsonl faithfully reflects the database, so hand-editing the export would falsify it rather than fix it. Surfaced by a local CodeRabbit pass, which read the gap as an inconsistent record and proposed patching the export; that remedy would have been wrong.
acceptance_criteria: bd reopen writes a field_change interaction recording the old status and the new one, the way bd close and bd update --status already do.
notes:
Resolved as an upstream defect, not stencil's to fix.

The bug is real and reproduced on bd 1.2.2 (6c124203e): create an issue,
`bd close` it, `bd reopen` it. The journal holds only `open -> closed`; the
issue's status is then `open` with no second record. `bd close` and
`bd update --status` both journal a field_change; `bd reopen` does not.

Nothing in this repository can fix it. bd is an external binary at
~/.local/bin/bd; its source is github.com/steveyegge/beads (vendored as
github.com/gastownhall/beads), and there is no local checkout. Editing
.beads/interactions.jsonl would not fix it either -- that file is a generated
export of the beads database, so hand-editing desynchronises the two rather
than repairing either.

Consequence to be aware of while it stands: any reopened issue's audit trail
shows a transition out of a state it was never recorded as leaving. stn-49v is
the example -- open -> in_progress -> closed, then open -> in_progress with
nothing bridging closed -> open.

Worth reporting upstream if the audit trail matters. Left closed here rather
than open, because an open ticket in stencil's tracker implies work stencil
can do, and there is none.
close_reason: Upstream bd defect (1.2.2), not fixable in this repository; no local beads checkout and the export is generated. Reproduction and consequences recorded in notes.

title: STENCIL.md documents copy_files, which stencil does not implement
description:
STENCIL.md:227 lists a per-package `copy_files` field -- 'Static files/dirs to copy from a files directory' -- and cs425's .config.yaml repeats it in its own comment block. There is no copy logic anywhere in stencil: `grep -rn copy stencil/*.py` returns nothing.

So the key is inert. Setting it produces no error and no files, which is the failure mode the config validation was built to prevent for template_env keys and `when:` names -- a typo that reads and writes nothing.

Found while adding config-level brand, where copy_files looked like the obvious mechanism to reuse and turned out not to exist. The brand work grew its own copying rather than waiting on this.

Two ways out, and they are genuinely different features:

- Implement it: a general per-package static-file copy, which brand's copying would then be one caller of.
- Delete the row from STENCIL.md and the comment from any consuming config, and let brand's copying stay the only thing that copies.

Whichever, the docs and the code have to agree.
notes:
Resolved by deleting the documentation rather than implementing the field.

Nothing asked for copy_files. The one thing that wanted to copy a file --
a config-level brand logo, added in 0.10.0 -- needed to copy implicitly
and register the copy in the managed .gitignore, neither of which a
general opt-in list gives you. Building the general mechanism to serve
one caller that does not want its shape is how you get a second inert
key.

If a second caller turns up, that is the moment to build it, with two
real uses to shape the interface instead of one guess.

title: A deck's title prints at the same size as a slide heading, depending on whether course is set
description:
In the deck print block, .slide > h1:first-child is 20pt. The generated title slide's

is that first child whenever the frontmatter has no course:, so the deck title prints at 20pt -- the same size as an ordinary slide heading, against 2.9rem on screen where it is clearly dominant. Set course: in the frontmatter and

becomes the first child, the h1 is no longer :first-child, and the title keeps 2.9rem (34.8pt) in print. So a deck's printed title size depends on an unrelated frontmatter key, invisibly. Measured: a deck with no course: printed its title at 26.7 (20pt) and its slide heading at 26.7. .deck-title and .deck-subtitle have no print rule of their own. Found while auditing the document title block for the same class of defect (stn-09g). Not fixed there because deck print typography is a design decision with no reported symptom, unlike the document inversion -- a flattened hierarchy rather than an inverted one.
acceptance_criteria: A deck's title prints larger than a slide heading, and its printed size does not change when course: is added or removed. Asserted against a real PDF.
notes:
Fixed in 8f0356c, on branch frontmatter-render-context.

The diagnosis in the description was right about the symptom and wrong
about the medium. It is not a print bug: `.slide > h1:first-child` scores
(0,2,1) against `.slide--title .deck-title`'s (0,2,0), so the heading rule
outranked the title rule on screen too. Screen looked correct only because
the decks that were eyeballed had a context line above the title, which
made the h1 not :first-child. Print was where it got noticed because the
print block restates the size in pt, so the gap was 20pt vs 34.8pt rather
than 1.75rem vs 2.9rem.

The fix is the exclusion, in both media, rather than a restated size:

    .slide:not(.slide--title) > h1:first-child,
    .slide:not(.slide--title) > h2:first-child,
    .slide:not(.slide--title) > h3:first-child

An explicit print size for .deck-title was tried first and reverted -- it
would have been a second scale to keep in step with the first, which is the
defect class 0.6.0 removed from the document side.

Acceptance criteria, both asserted against a real PDF in
tests/test_frontmatter.py:

- test_a_deck_title_prints_larger_than_a_slide_heading, parametrized on the
  context key being present or absent
- test_the_deck_title_prints_the_same_size_either_way, which is the
  "does not change" half stated on its own

Both read every page rather than page one: a deck prints one slide per
page, so the title is on page 1 and the heading it must outrank is on
page 2.

One deviation from the criteria as written: the key is `program:`, not
`course:`. The same commit removed the package-name-as-course injection
and replaced it with author-set program/section/term, so `course` no
longer exists as a key. The invariant is unchanged -- the printed title
size does not depend on the context line -- and the tests are parametrized
on `program:` accordingly.

title: Nothing checks the contract between stencil's partials and a consumer's composition
description:
cs234 overrides stencil's Makefile.j2 and docker-compose.yml.j2 and composes them out of stencil's partials -- Makefile-base.j2, Makefile-doc.j2, Makefile-pkg.j2, docker-compose-html.yml.j2 -- through {% include %}. That layering is the search path working as designed, and it is what TEMPLATE-PACKS.md would formalise.

The problem is that the contract is unwritten and unchecked. cs234's Makefile.j2 is 200 lines composed against variables those partials happen to define today. Rename one in stencil and cs234 renders a Makefile that is subtly wrong, with nothing failing in either repository -- a missing recipe or an empty variable, discovered when someone runs make.

This is the failure that can actually reach a handout, and it is why the pack design says a pack is not a fix for it.

Shape worth exploring: name the variables each partial requires, and test that a partial rendered in isolation fails loudly when one is absent rather than expanding to the empty string.
acceptance_criteria: The variables each shared partial requires of its includer are written down, and a test fails when a partial stops providing one or starts requiring a new one. It should fail in stencil's own suite, not only in a consumer.
close_reason: Two guards. tests/test_template_contract.py records what each shared partial reads and fails when that changes; the Jinja environment uses StrictUndefined so an unknown name raises at gen time instead of rendering empty. Mutation-verified: renaming package_stem to pkg_stem in Makefile-pkg.j2 fails stencil's own contract test AND makes cs234 fail loudly with 'pkg_stem is undefined' rather than emitting a Makefile with a hole. A key set by some packages defaults to lenient Undefined, not False -- False satisfies | default(...) and put the literal 'False' into generated TypeScript where a filename belonged, caught by the consumer diff before it shipped.

title: Reject a template_env key that no template declares
description:
get_template_context does context.update(template_env), so any key is accepted, and a `when:` naming a key nobody set reads as None. A typo -- has_vscde instead of has_vscode -- renders nothing and reports nothing, which is how a package quietly loses its .vscode settings.

cs234 drives has_vscode and has_install_scripts through this path today, so the failure is live rather than hypothetical.

Worth doing on its own, independent of template packs: TEMPLATE-PACKS.md reaches the same conclusion from the other direction, since a pack has to declare the keys it reads before stencil can validate against them.
acceptance_criteria: A config whose template_env sets a key that no template's `when:` references, or whose `when:` names a key nothing sets, fails with a message naming the key. Existing configs that spell their keys correctly are unaffected.
notes:
Correction after review. The unread-key half of this was first implemented as 'no when: names it and no template reads it', using jinja2.meta.find_undeclared_variables. That is unsound: a custom key need not reach a template as a variable. cs234's nginx.conf.j2 reads three of them as dict lookups -- (template_env | default({})).get('docroot_subdir') -- which no analysis of variable names can see, and stencil gen would have rejected answers/.config.yaml outright. It now asks only whether the name appears anywhere in any template, as a loaded name or a string constant, which is the strongest claim that can be made soundly.

Separately, CodeRabbit found that a dynamic {% include some_var %} is reported by Jinja as a reference of None. The scan now tracks whether it saw the whole tree and suspends the unread-key check when it did not, because a false rejection blocks a correct config while a missed typo does not.

Both were caught only by running the real consumer configs through the CLI; the test suite was green for both.

title: Generated pages depend on CDNs at PDF time, making builds network-bound
description: embed-images.lua inlines local images, but Bootstrap, highlight.js, Mermaid and the Google webfonts are all fetched at page load. html-to-pdf.js correctly refuses to write a PDF when any request fails, so 'make pdf' cannot run offline and fails on a transient CDN error. Observed repeatedly as net::ERR_NETWORK_CHANGED inside the container while running the PDF suite; the host reached the same URLs in 70ms, so it is container-network churn rather than a real outage. tests/conftest.py retries up to five times to work around it. The real fix is to vendor the assets into the browser image or inline them at build time, which would also make a generated handout genuinely self-contained -- AUTHORING.md already promises 'one self-contained file', which is only true of the images today.

title: Warn authors that mdformat corrupts stencil-dialect markdown
description: AUTHORING.md has a 'Fenced divs and prettier' section warning about one formatter but says nothing about mdformat, which is strictly more destructive. Pointing mdformat at a document or deck rewrites YAML front matter into a thematic break plus a heading, turns the '---' slide separator into '______' (destroying slide splitting), and escapes LaTeX backslashes so '\\lambda' becomes '\\\\lambda' -- the last one being invisible in review and fatal to the math. Found when mdformat mangled tests/fixtures/. stencil's own hook now excludes them, but a consuming project that runs mdformat over its course content gets no warning at all.

title: Commits can capture a stale .beads/issues.jsonl when bd writes and pre-commit overlap
description:
Twice in one session a commit landed with an issue export that was behind the Dolt database. PR #9 was needed because two 'bd close' calls ran after the last commit; PR #11 because a commit captured 87 issues when the database held 90, silently dropping three new tasks and three notes from what the PR claimed to add.

Two distinct causes, one symptom:

1. bd writes that happen after the final commit of a change simply never get exported into it. Closing issues in the same shell invocation as a merge does this every time.
2. The pre-commit framework stashes unstaged changes before running hooks and restores them afterwards, while beads' own git pre-commit hook rewrites .beads/issues.jsonl inside that window. The staged snapshot can be taken before beads finishes.

The second is the dangerous one, because the working tree looks clean afterwards. Nothing warns that git and the database disagree, and the export is the only view most reviewers get.

Worth considering: a bd doctor check or a pre-push hook that compares 'bd export' output against the committed file and refuses to push on drift. That turns a silent divergence into a loud one, which is all it needs to be.
acceptance_criteria: Either a check that fails when the committed export differs from a fresh 'bd export', or a documented rule in AGENTS.md about ordering bd writes relative to commits. A deliberate divergence must be detected rather than merging silently.

title: Track generated PDFs in get_generated_files so clean and install cover them
description:

title: Add a pdf compose service that prints generated HTML through headless Chromium
description:
Create stencil/templates/docker-compose-pdf.yml.j2 defining a 'pdf' service, and include it from docker-compose.yml.j2 alongside the existing docker-compose-html.yml.j2 include.

The service takes an HTML path and an output PDF path and drives headless Chromium through a Puppeteer script. A bare 'chromium --headless --print-to-pdf' is not sufficient: Mermaid renders client-side and _page-scripts.html.j2 assembles the tab structure only after the 'mermaid-ready' event fires, so an immediate capture emits raw mermaid source in a code block and unbuilt tabs.

The script must await window.__mermaidReady and document.fonts.ready, then call page.pdf({ preferCSSPageSize: true, printBackground: true }). preferCSSPageSize picks up the @page rules already in _page-style.css.j2 (letter, 1in margins) and _slide-style.css.j2 (letter landscape, one slide per page). printBackground preserves the print-color-adjust: exact declarations on table headers, row stripes, blockquotes, and slide title bars.

Because the pages load Bootstrap, highlight.js, Mermaid, and Google Fonts from CDNs, the service needs network egress and must fail loudly on a failed asset request or a ready signal that never arrives. Silently emitting an unstyled PDF would contradict the --fail-if-warnings stance the pandoc services take deliberately.

The check-access service in docker-compose-html.yml.j2 is the container precedent: node:lts-alpine, chromium via apk, PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true and PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/usr/bin/chromium-browser already set, with --no-sandbox / --disable-dev-shm-usage launch args.
acceptance_criteria: A generated docker-compose.yml contains a pdf service. Running it against a generated HTML file produces a PDF whose page size and margins match the @page rules, with rendered Mermaid SVG, expanded tab panes, and preserved background colors. A page whose assets fail to load or whose ready signal never fires exits non-zero instead of writing a PDF.

title: Add a 'make pdf' target that converts generated HTML to PDF
description:
Reintroduce PDF output, but as a post-processing stage over the HTML build rather than a parallel pandoc/LaTeX pipeline. 'make pdf' depends on 'doc' and converts each HTML file that was generated from a markdown source into a PDF of the same basename with a .pdf extension.

Design decisions already settled:
- No config surface. The target is emitted for every package where has_pages is true, exactly like 'doc'. It is always available and only runs when explicitly invoked. There is no 'pdfs:' list and no 'has_pdfs' flag -- the removed schema is not coming back.
- Conversion is headless Chromium, not a PDF-specific pandoc/LaTeX pipeline. The print CSS already in _page-style.css.j2 and _slide-style.css.j2 IS the page layout engine: documents already declare @page { size: letter; margin: 1in } with page-break-inside: avoid on pre/blockquote/table/figure, and decks already declare @page { size: letter landscape } with break-after: page per slide. Chromium's print-to-PDF honors both, so no new layout code is needed.
- WITH= variants must pair correctly. Session1-hidden.html produces Session1-hidden.pdf; the target has to thread $(OUTPUT_SUFFIX) through rather than assuming the plain build.

Two known hazards drive the subtasks:
1. The generated HTML is NOT self-contained. embed-images.lua inlines images only; _page-head.html.j2 and _page-scripts.html.j2 load Bootstrap, highlight.js, Mermaid, and Google Fonts from CDNs at page load. The PDF container needs network egress, and a CDN failure would otherwise silently emit an unstyled PDF -- which contradicts the --fail-if-warnings philosophy the pandoc stage is deliberate about.
2. Content is built client-side. Mermaid renders in the browser and the tab structure is assembled by JS waiting on the 'mermaid-ready' event. A bare 'chromium --headless --print-to-pdf' captures the page before any of that runs and would emit raw mermaid source inside a code block.
design: Conversion runs through a Puppeteer script rather than 'chromium --print-to-pdf' so it can await window.__mermaidReady and document.fonts.ready before calling page.pdf({ preferCSSPageSize: true, printBackground: true }). preferCSSPageSize honors the existing @page rules; printBackground honors the print-color-adjust: exact declarations on table headers, stripes, blockquotes, and slide title bars. The existing check-access service is the precedent for the container shape: node:lts-alpine with chromium added via apk and PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD / PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH already set.
acceptance_criteria: 'make pdf' exists in every generated package that renders markdown, depends on doc (and slide where applicable), and produces one PDF per generated HTML with the same basename. 'make pdf with=hidden' pairs the -hidden HTML with the -hidden PDF. Mermaid diagrams appear as rendered SVG and tabbed sections appear fully expanded in the PDF. A failed CDN asset or a page whose JS never signals ready fails the build rather than emitting a degraded PDF. 'stencil clean' removes generated PDFs and 'stencil install' gitignores them. Verified by generating a scratch package and running the pipeline end to end, per AGENTS.md. Lands via pull request.

## Architecture Overview

**stencil is a scaffolding generator, not a renderer.** It never invokes pandoc.
`generate.py` renders Jinja2 templates into per-package output directories; the
`Makefile` and `docker-compose.yml` it emits are what actually run pandoc.

Templates resolve through a search path — every `templates_dir` in config order, then
the bundled `stencil/templates/`, first match wins — so a consuming project overrides
one template without vendoring the set.

Under `stencil/templates/`: two pandoc HTML templates (`html-template` for flowing
documents, `slides-template` for decks), shared partials (`_page-head`, `_page-style`,
`_page-scripts`) that both include, deck-only partials (`_slides-*`), and the Lua
filters that do the real work — `hidden-filter` (WITH= variants), `mermaid-figure-filter`
(figure/figcaption), `embed-images` (base64 inlining), `slide-sections` (slide grouping).

title: Painted gaps outside the header have never been checked in the text layer
description:
stn-40n established that a whitespace-only text node between two inline boxes never reaches the PDF text layer, and that a gap painted by margin, flex gap or generated content leaves no character behind. 0.13.0 applied that to the document and deck headers only.

The same shape exists elsewhere and is unasserted:

- `.side-by-side { gap: 2rem }` (_page-style.css.j2) puts two tables' text on one baseline behind a painted gap.
- `.columns { gap: 1.75rem }` (_slide-style.css.j2) does the same for two prose columns on a slide.
- `header.doc-title` is a grid with `column-gap: 1.5rem`; identity and context sit in two columns on one baseline. They stay apart in the extracted text today because they are far apart in the content stream, not because a character separates them. tests/test_pdf.py asserts that they do not run together, so a change here fails a test rather than a printout -- but the guard is weaker than the others in that file and says so.
- The facts line's accessibility boundary comes from `.doc-facts` being `display: flex` -- its children blockify -- rather than from any character. Its separators are aria-hidden and contribute no whitespace, so Chromium's accessibility tree gives 'Sep 05' adjacent to 'Due'. Pre-existing since 0.11.0. The stylesheet now records that the flex is load-bearing for this and not only for layout; nothing enforces it.

Measure each in a real PDF before deciding which need fixing. Fixing the facts line means putting a character inside each flex item, which shifts the space-between distribution -- a rendered change needing its own measurement.

title: Check the PDFs for PDF/UA conformance, not just for the defects we found
description:
0.13.0 added the first checks in this repository that look at a PDF: the header extracts as words, the document is tagged, declares its language, and sets DisplayDocTitle. That is a floor, not conformance. It asserts the handful of properties measured while fixing stn-40n, and it would not notice a missing alt text on a figure, an untagged table, a heading level skipped in the structure tree, or a reading order that disagrees with the visual one.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE, so the cost is judgeable without re-deriving it:

- veraPDF is the reference PDF/UA checker and it is a Java application. The browser image (Dockerfile.browser.j2) currently installs Chromium, puppeteer and pa11y on node; adding a JRE plus veraPDF is a second toolchain and a materially bigger image, on an image that is already slow enough to be built once per test session.
- A conformance profile has to be argued with rather than adopted. Chromium's tagged output is not PDF/UA-1 clean out of the box -- expect findings about the document being untagged-by-parts, artifact classification of running headers, and figure alt text that has no HTML source to come from. Each is a decision about what stencil should emit, not a bug to fix mechanically.
- Alt text is the likely blocker. mermaid-figure-filter.lua produces figures with captions; PDF/UA wants /Alt on the figure structure element, and Chromium derives that from HTML alt attributes. Getting that right is its own piece of work.
- It wants a make target (check-access-pdf, beside the existing check-access) and a CI job, which means the PDF build has to run in CI -- it currently does not.

Worth doing before anyone claims the PDFs are accessible for compliance rather than for printing. Not worth folding into a spacing fix.

Acceptance: a PDF/UA check runs in the repository against a generated handout and a generated deck, its findings are either clean or explicitly triaged in writing, and CI runs it.

MEASURED DEPENDENCY SURFACE (stencil 0.11.0)

Inlined into every generated page:
  bootstrap.min.css        227.3 KB
  bootstrap.bundle.min.js   78.8 KB
                           ------- 306.1 KB

What that buys, in full:
  - `.container`, used twice in the templates -- and stencil overrides its
    max-width to 60rem anyway, so only the horizontal padding survives.
  - Reboot/normalize: box-sizing, margin resets, default table and form
    rendering.
  - `bootstrap.Tab`, one JS call, for the tabbed-sections feature:
    `bootstrap.Tab.getOrCreateInstance(trigger).show()`, the
    data-bs-toggle/data-bs-target attributes, and the `shown.bs.tab` event.
  - The runtime classes the tab code writes: nav, nav-tabs, nav-link,
    tab-content, tab-pane, fade, show, active.

What it does NOT buy, because stencil already owns it:
  - body, h1-h6, blockquote, code, pre
  - table, thead, tbody, th, td, and the even-row striping
  - .nav-tabs.problem-tabs, .tab-content, .tab-pane -- stencil restyles the
    tab chrome itself
  - every print rule
  - ZERO --bs-* custom properties are consumed by stencil's own CSS
    (grep count: 0 in both stylesheets)

So 306 KB per page is buying a container's padding, a CSS reset, and a
show/hide widget.

WHY MATERIAL UI IS THE WRONG TARGET

MUI is a React component library, not a CSS framework. It needs React,
ReactDOM and Emotion at runtime. Pandoc emits static HTML; there is no React
tree for MUI to render into. Adopting it would mean:

  - Shipping React + ReactDOM + Emotion inline, so page weight goes UP, not
    down, to replace 306 KB that is mostly unused.
  - Rewriting the tab feature as a client-side React island mounted into
    pandoc's output.
  - Emotion injecting <style> at runtime. That is directly hostile to the
    theming design (stn-pci), whose entire print guarantee is that every dark
    declaration is sealed inside @media screen where the print formatter
    cannot see it. Runtime-injected styles are not in that stylesheet.
  - A hydration barrier ahead of window.__mermaidReady, which html-to-pdf.js
    blocks on before printing. That handshake is the most fragile part of the
    build.
  - Still no document typography: MUI styles components, not prose, headings
    or tables, which is what a handout is made of.

Material Web (@material/web), Google's own M3 web components, avoids React but
is also a poor fit: it is ESM-only and stencil's vendor pipeline inlines
single pre-built files with no bundler, and its custom elements are
interactive widgets rather than a document stylesheet. It would replace the
tab widget and nothing else.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE, IF THIS IS EVER WANTED

Take Material Design 3 as a design system rather than as a component library,
and drop Bootstrap outright:

  1. Adopt the M3 color roles, type scale and elevation levels as CSS custom
     properties. This is the same token layer stn-pci already builds; M3 would
     supply the values rather than a second mechanism.
  2. Write the reset and container rules stencil actually needs -- on the
     order of 40 lines, since it already styles everything else.
  3. Replace bootstrap.Tab with vanilla JS: show/hide panes, manage
     aria-selected and roving tabindex, dispatch one custom event where
     `shown.bs.tab` is currently awaited. Roughly 30 lines.

Net effect: -306 KB per generated page, one styling mechanism instead of two,
and no framework runtime.

SEQUENCING

After stn-pci, not before. That work creates the token layer this would
populate; doing it first means writing the token layer twice and reconciling
them.

RISK THE TEST SUITE CANNOT SEE

Dropping Reboot changes rendering in ways this suite is structurally blind to
-- it asserts DOM structure and stylesheet text, and both are unchanged by a
normalization rule that quietly disappears. That blind spot produced two
defects during 0.11.0: a dropped grid rule and a 3.88:1 contrast failure, both
past a green suite and a green CI matrix. Any attempt at this needs rendered
evidence, before and after: PDF page-break positions, table rendering, and
`make check-access` green in both themes.
acceptance_criteria: No bootstrap.min.css or bootstrap.bundle.min.js in stencil/assets or in a generated page. Tabbed sections still work: keyboard navigation, aria-selected, deep links into a hidden pane, and whatever event html-to-pdf.js waits on. make check-access green in both themes. Rendered before/after evidence for page breaks and table rendering in PDF, not just a passing suite. Page weight reduced by at least 250 KB.

title: Design template packs so a course repo depends on its scaffolding instead of vendoring it
description:
cs234/_generator/templates is a second template pack living outside the tool:
ten entries covering Playwright grading specs, a MySQL grading runner and its db
directory, nginx configuration including a view-source variant, a Dockerfile, an
install directory, and vscode settings. None of it is course content and none of
it is stencil's -- it is scaffolding a course repo needs that stencil has no
opinion about.

stn-z8w removed the bundled PHP, MySQL and Nginx templates from stencil on the
grounds that they belonged to a consumer rather than the tool. That call was
right, and this ticket is not asking to undo it. What it left behind is the
other half of the problem: the consumer now maintains a generator of its own,
duplicating the walk-config-render loop stencil already implements, and every
improvement to stencil's rendering has to be reimplemented there or go without.

The shape worth exploring is a template pack a course repo depends on rather
than vendors: stencil keeps the engine and the markdown pipeline, a pack
supplies its own templates and config schema, and cs234 and cs425 each name the
pack they use. That makes the grading infrastructure a versioned dependency
instead of a directory that drifts.

Open questions this needs answered before any code:
  - Where does a pack live -- its own repository, a directory convention, an
    entry point?
  - How does a pack extend the config schema without stencil knowing its keys?
  - What does a pack get to override, and what stays stencil's?
  - Does the existing `templates:` config list become a pack, so there is one
    mechanism rather than two?

This is a design question with a real blast radius across at least two course
repos, so it should be planned before it is built, and it should come after the
smaller items are settled.

Note on the ordering: an earlier draft justified waiting on stn-aig by arguing a
pack should not depend on an untagged tool. That argument is dead -- the
maintainer has ruled out pinning stencil in consuming repos, and stn-aig is now
about tags as a reference point rather than a consumer contract. The dependency
stands anyway, for the plainer reason that this is the largest item and should
follow the smaller ones. A pack must not reintroduce pinning through the back
door: whatever depends on a pack should be free to track it the way course repos
track stencil today.

Raised by an external review of the repository.
acceptance_criteria:
A written design, agreed before implementation, covering where a pack lives, how
it extends the config schema, what it may override, and whether stencil's
existing `templates:` list collapses into the same mechanism. A migration path
for cs234/_generator/templates that does not require a flag day across course
repos.
close_reason: Design written in TEMPLATE-PACKS.md, answering all four questions plus a migration path in four independently-shippable steps. Two of the ticket's premises were wrong and are corrected there: cs234 has no generator of its own (only templates/, rendered by stencil), and cs425 has templates_dir commented out, so the radius is one repo. Recommendation is to not build yet, with the trigger written down -- a second repository needing those templates. Follow-ups filed as stn-806 (declare template_env keys) and stn-e2l (the partial/composition contract, the failure that can actually reach a handout).

title: Decide whether the export-drift guard's test weight is earning its keep
description:
tests/test_export_drift.py is the largest test file in the repository and it
tests the tracker's git hygiene rather than anything stencil generates. An
external review asked whether the pre-push guard is earning that.

The question is fair and the answer is not obvious, so this is a review rather
than a removal.

What argues for keeping it: during the session that hardened the guard it caught
two real divergences that nothing else would have -- a database that had
regressed to an earlier snapshot, and a history rewrite that changed a committed
blob without touching the database. It also turned up that the hook had never
run on the maintainer's machine at all, because the wrapper was gated on
`command -v pre-commit`. None of that would have surfaced without the guard.

What argues against: the file grew substantially while fixing those, and every
line of it is about beads bookkeeping. A reader looking for what stencil does
finds the largest test file in the repo is about something else. There is also a
real question of whether this belongs in stencil at all rather than in beads or
in a shared hook package -- nothing about it is specific to this project.

Decide between:
  - Keep as is, and write down why the cost is accepted.
  - Trim to the cases that have actually fired, dropping the defensive ones.
  - Move the guard and its tests out of stencil entirely.

Do not remove coverage without deciding the first question. The guard's value
was demonstrated after the review was written, and the review did not have that
evidence.
acceptance_criteria:
A decision is recorded, with reasons, on one of: keep, trim, or relocate. If
trimmed or relocated, the drift guard still fails a push when the committed
export and the database disagree, and a test proves it.
close_reason: Decision: keep, recorded with reasons in AGENTS.md. The deciding evidence is the guard catching the hook not running at all on the maintainer's machine -- a guard that fails open is worse than none, and only a test finds that. Trimming rejected because the cases that fired were not the predicted ones; relocating to beads or a shared hook package is right in principle but would make stencil depend on something that does not exist, with a second repository needing the guard as the trigger to revisit. No coverage removed.

title: pre-commit hook hardcodes an INSTALL_PYTHON path from another machine
description: .beads/hooks/pre-commit is generated by the pre-commit framework and sets INSTALL_PYTHON=<repo>/.venv/bin/python3.14 -- a macOS path, in a repo being worked on from Linux at <home>. The file is tracked, so every clone gets it. Nothing breaks today because the hook falls through to 'command -v pre-commit', but that silently depends on a venv being active: commit with no venv and the hooks are skipped rather than failing loudly. The path also cannot be right for two contributors at once. Regenerating it is not straightforward because 'pre-commit install' refuses to run while core.hooksPath points at .beads/hooks, which is why the pre-push chain added in stn-cix was written by hand and deliberately omits INSTALL_PYTHON.
close_reason: The hook now resolves the repo's venv from its own location (PRE_COMMIT_PYTHON overrides), so no contributor's absolute path is tracked. tests/test_hooks.py guards every hook against reintroduction.

title: A missing .config.yaml exits with a traceback instead of an error message
description: Running any stencil subcommand outside a configured project prints a FileNotFoundError traceback from load_config rather than a one-line error naming the missing file and suggesting 'stencil init' or the expected path. Pre-existing; noticed while verifying the pipeline extraction. load_config should catch FileNotFoundError and exit non-zero with a readable message.
close_reason: load_config now exits with a message naming the file for a missing, unreadable, empty or malformed config. Covered by tests/test_cli.py.

title: make doc reports Generated docs for a package that has no docs
description:
In `stencil/templates/Makefile-doc.j2` the closing

    @echo "Generated docs$(if $(WITH), with features: $(WITH),)"

sits outside the `{% if has_docs %} ... {% endif %}` guard that wraps the pandoc
invocations above it. A package that declares only slides therefore builds a deck and
then reports that it generated docs.

It compounds with `doc` depending on `slide`. For a slides-only package, `make doc` runs
format-md, builds the deck, and prints "Generated docs" — so the output claims a document
was produced, the only HTML on disk is a deck, and nothing says otherwise. Someone
reasonably concludes the doc pipeline emitted a deck and goes looking for a bug in the
templates or the filter chain, which is where the real cost is.

Observed on the cs425 `notes` package while it was configured slides-only.

Fix: move the echo inside the `has_docs` guard, or better, have each branch report what
it actually built. The `slide` target already prints "Generated slides" correctly, so the
`doc` target is the odd one out.

Cosmetic in isolation. Filed because the cost is misdirected debugging rather than a
wrong artifact.
close_reason: Moved the closing echo inside the has_docs guard and made the help text conditional on both flags. Two regression tests, verified to fail against the previous template.

title: Prebuild the pdf service image instead of installing Chromium on every run
description:
The pdf service installs Chromium via apk and Puppeteer via npm each time it runs, adding roughly 12 seconds per file. It follows the existing check-access pattern, which does the same thing, so this is consistent rather than novel -- but a package with a dozen documents pays it a dozen times.

Options: a Dockerfile.pdf.j2 built once per package (the old LaTeX pipeline used a per-package build this way), a shared prebuilt image published somewhere, or caching the apk/npm layers in a named volume. Worth measuring before choosing; the npm install may dominate the apk add or vice versa.

Applies to check-access equally, so whatever is chosen should probably cover both.
acceptance_criteria: make pdf spends no meaningful time installing dependencies on a warm cache. The chosen approach is applied consistently to check-access as well, or a reason is recorded for why it is not.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #8. Shared Dockerfile.browser image for the pdf and check-access services cuts a single PDF conversion from ~12s to 2.3s; package-data no longer lists nonexistent directories, and clearing the stale build/ tree stopped pip install from shipping deleted LaTeX templates.

title: pyproject package-data lists files/ and scripts/ directories that do not exist
description:
[tool.setuptools.package-data] declares stencil = [..., "files/.vscode/*", "scripts/*"]. Neither stencil/files/ nor stencil/scripts/ exists in the repository. They were the backing store for the copy_files and deps_script config fields, which generate.py also never implemented; those fields were removed from config.example.yaml in the stn-bai change.

Harmless at build time (setuptools skips missing globs) but misleading: it implies a static-file copying feature the generator does not have. Remove the two entries, or implement copy_files/deps_script if the feature is actually wanted -- decide which before touching it.
acceptance_criteria: pyproject.toml package-data lists only paths that exist, or the copy_files/deps_script feature is implemented in generate.py and the directories exist. Lands via pull request.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #8. Shared Dockerfile.browser image for the pdf and check-access services cuts a single PDF conversion from ~12s to 2.3s; package-data no longer lists nonexistent directories, and clearing the stale build/ tree stopped pip install from shipping deleted LaTeX templates.

title: Document the pdf target across the guides and the example config
description:
Once 'make pdf' exists, the guides need to describe it and distinguish it from the browser print path that already exists.

- STENCIL.md: the Printing section currently tells the reader to use Ctrl+P / Cmd+P. Add 'make pdf' as the scripted equivalent and make clear both routes go through the same print CSS, so the output matches.
- AUTHORING.md: the 'Printing a deck' section needs the same treatment for slide decks.
- README.md: add pdf to the documented make targets.
- config.example.yaml: note that pdf is always available for packages that render markdown and needs no configuration. This is what the file should say AFTER the stale LaTeX schema is removed -- see the blocking issue.
- AGENTS.md: the existing 'pandoc filter order is load-bearing' section documents ordering constraints nothing in the build enforces. The PDF stage adds a sibling constraint worth recording in the same spirit: the print CSS in _page-style.css.j2 and _slide-style.css.j2 is not cosmetic, it is the PDF page layout engine, so a change to @page or the break-* rules changes PDF pagination and not just what Ctrl+P produces.
acceptance_criteria: All five files describe the pdf target consistently, and the relationship between make pdf and browser printing is stated once and clearly rather than implied.
close_reason: Documented make pdf in STENCIL.md (Printing and PDFs), AUTHORING.md (command list and Printing a deck), README.md (targets, package types, bundled templates), config.example.yaml (needs no configuration), and AGENTS.md (new section: the print stylesheet is the PDF page geometry). Also corrected the stale 'make slides' target name in AUTHORING.md.
